summary: A reply to RFC 86, which proposed a standard way to send graphics over the network. The author at Ames Research Center agrees that sending a device-independent description and converting it at the receiving host is sound. The main objection is that the proposal ignores many features of real graphics devices.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a picture as instructions that any machine can follow is a good idea, this 1971 reply says. The writer agrees with the plan but asks for switches that turn extra features on, better handling of text, and a way to work out what a person has pointed at on the screen.

questions: is a device-independent graphics format a good idea
what were the objections to rfc 86
what is a network graphics data stream
what are mode primitives for graphics
subtitle: A 1971 reply to the graphics data stream proposal: sound idea, but add modes, richer text and picture interaction.

tldr.problem: RFC 86 proposed a network standard format for a graphics data stream, but the author felt the proposal took no account of the many features of real graphics devices.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes separate mode primitives, form control characters inside strings, a display list pointer, an include list primitive, commands to manipulate a list and a way to report what a user points at.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of comments rather than a specification, and it asks for more discussion of how a user interacts with a displayed picture.

today: The unit metadata says RFC 125 updates RFC 86 and is updated by RFC 177. It is a set of comments, and the text does not claim that its proposals were adopted.

sections.title: Support for the Approach
sections.content:
John McConnell of Ames Research Center wrote in answer to RFC 86. He said the basic approach, sending an intermediate, device-independent language and translating it into specific device codes at the receiving host, is sound. In his view it is the only approach that lets people concentrate on describing pictures.

Ames Research Center had adopted the approach to connect its various graphics devices and computers. At the time of writing it was in the design phase and expected its package to be running in about six months.
sections.plainLanguage: The writer agrees that sending picture instructions rather than a finished picture is the right plan, and notes that his own lab is already building it.

sections.title: Modes and Character Strings
sections.content:
The main objection is that the proposed structure ignores the many features of graphics devices. The memo proposes mode primitives, logically separate from the drawing primitives of RFC 86. A mode acts on the drawing primitives that follow and lasts until another mode primitive resets it. If a feature is missing at a host, the interpreter can treat the mode as a null operation. Modes could control intensity levels or colour, add blinking, and, for vectors, draw dashed lines.

For character strings, the memo strongly objects to leaving out form control characters, which could handle upper and lower case, subscripting, superscripting, underscoring and tab motion. It lists the controls it would use: backspace, new line, shift case, superscript, subscript, a marker for a special non-ASCII character, and tab. It also asks for size and orientation options, and for some way to define symbols that are not in ASCII, either by a control code plus a 16-bit list name or by allowing 8-bit characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Drawing commands should stay simple, with separate switches for extras such as colour, blinking and dashed lines. Text should be able to carry small signals for things like raised or lowered letters.

sections.title: Display Lists and Manipulation
sections.content:
The memo adds a display list pointer (NGDLP). Its value is a displacement from the head of a list and names the next drawing primitive to run. When an execute list primitive is reached, the current pointer is saved along with the list name and the current origin, and the saved values are restored when that list finishes.

An include list primitive would treat a sub-list as a macro rather than a subroutine, so changing one sub-list would not change every sub-picture on the screen. To reduce the amount of data sent, extra commands parsed by the interpreter would let the receiving host rescale coordinates, move the origin or rotate a list, and show or hide a list or enable and disable light pen detection without sending it again.
sections.plainLanguage: A bookmark records which drawing step comes next, and a small picture can be copied into a larger one. Those commands also let the far machine shrink, move or turn a picture without sending the whole thing again.

sections.title: Interacting with the Picture
sections.content:
The memo notes that interaction with the displayed picture had not yet been addressed, and it tries to start that discussion. A keyboard or function keys are no problem, because they can be handled as a standard message from the graphics terminal. Devices that interact with the picture or screen, such as light pens, mice, joysticks or tablets, are harder, because the point selected has to be tied to a meaningful list or primitive. The memo argues this tie should be made at the receiving host, since the data stream arriving there may have changed in unknown ways.

To let the sending host identify the object pointed at, the stack of suspended lists and the current pointer value would qualify it at any level of the hierarchy, together with normalised x,y coordinates and a character displacement if a string was pointed at. Where no beam motion occurs, a sub-list run periodically might be needed to find the light pen.
sections.plainLanguage: Pointing at a picture is difficult, because the computer must work out which part you meant. The writer asks others to help think it through.

references.text: Osanna, J., Sahzer, J., "Remote Terminal Character Stream Processing of Multics", Proceedings SJCC, 1970, p. 671.
